cues.text: Born when girls could not play
Formiga was born Miraildes Maciel Mota in 1978, in Salvador, Brazil.
When she was born, a law in Brazil said that women were not allowed to play football.
Girls who loved football had to play in secret, or not at all.
Flip the sign.
The law was removed in 1979, but for many years after that, girls who played football were still not taken seriously.
Formiga would help to change that.
An unfair rule can be changed. Keep playing, and help others play too.
Her mother said yes
When she was nine, Formiga’s family moved to Camaçari, near Salvador.
She began playing football at twelve.
Not everyone in her family wanted her to play.
Open the gate.
Her mother, Dona Celeste, took her to play futsal for a club called Euroexport.
With one person on her side, Formiga could start.
Formiga learned quick passing and close control in futsal, skills she used all through her life.
One person who believes in you can change everything.
Small and strong
Formiga means ant in Portuguese.
Someone watching one of her games said she looked like an ant, playing against bigger, older men.
She was small, and she ran all over the pitch.
Lift the flap.
Formiga has said she never liked the nickname, but it stayed with her for her whole career.
An ant is tiny, but it can carry heavy loads and never stops working.
Being small is not a weakness. Work hard and help your team, like an ant.
So close, again and again
Formiga first played for Brazil in 1995, when she was seventeen.
Brazil came close to the biggest prizes many times.
They lost the Olympic finals of 2004 and 2008 to the United States, and they finished second at the 2007 World Cup.
Getting so close and not winning can feel even harder than losing early.
Turn over the two medals.
Losing big finals is painful.
Each time, Formiga came back and played again.
She kept training, kept passing and kept helping the younger players around her.
Losing finals is hard. Coming back each time is what makes you strong.
Seven World Cups
Formiga played at seven World Cups, more than any other player.
In 2015, at thirty-seven, she became the oldest player to score at a Women’s World Cup.
In 2019, at forty-one, she became the oldest player ever at the tournament.
Most footballers stop playing long before forty.
Climb the steps.
She also played at seven Olympic Games, from 1996 to 2020.
No other footballer, man or woman, has played at seven World Cups and seven Olympics.
If you love the game and look after your body, you can play for a long time.
A long, long journey
In November 2021, Formiga played her last match for Brazil, at forty-three.
She had played for her country for twenty-six years, and 234 times, more than any other Brazilian footballer, man or woman.
She also played in France for Paris Saint-Germain, and at forty-one she became the oldest player to score in the Women’s Champions League.
Wave the flag.
The girl born when women were not allowed to play had become one of the greatest players in Brazil’s history.
Keep going, and you can open the way for the girls and boys who come after you.
